content.title: W 72nd Avenue Bond Project
content.summary: The W. 72nd Avenue restoration project, set to begin in August 2026, will include water line replacement, sidewalk repairs, and road repaving, with an expected completion time of 4 to 5 months. However, the City has decided to cancel the construction of an underpass due to significant cost escalations, with the project now estimated at $137 million, far exceeding the original bond amount of $64.5 million, prompting a reevaluation of funding and project feasibility.
content.body:
## Oak to Kipling Restoration Work

Updated 6/12/26

The contract for 2026 restoration work along W. 72nd Avenue from Oak Street to Kipling is on the agenda for the July 7 City Council meeting. Following contract approval, **work is expected to begin as soon as August.**

### Timeline

Work is expected to take **4 to 5****months** to complete. 

### Planned restoration work

- Water line replacement
- Oak intersection improvements
  - ADA curb ramps
  - Sidewalk and bike lane connections on the east side
- Sidewalk repairs on the north side of W 72nd
- Repaving the existing two-lane road (Oak to Lee Ct.)
- Repaving side streets via the Pavement Program (72nd Pl., 71st Pl., 70th Dr.)
  - See the map of work areas on the [Pavement Program webpage](/629)
- Replace street light bulbs to correct brightness issues
- North entrance improvements at Lincoln Academy
  - Sidewalk connections
  - W 72nd Ave left turn lane
  - Other / miscellaneous repairs
- Miscellaneous repairs and clean up throughout the corridor

## Update on Project Changes

Updated 1/21/26

Due to considerable cost escalation, the City has decided not to proceed with construction of the underpass at the railroad for the W. 72nd Avenue widening project.

1. [About the Decision](#tabc79cc707-4d40-46f1-9232-6faa0b70af92_0)

## Why this decision was made

The City received updated cost estimates in mid-December that brought the project total to $137M, more than double the original bond amount of $64.5M and nearly $40M more than the previous estimate of $97.5M, which had been incorporated into the City’s 10-year financial model.

## Key cost factors

- Extreme inflation in the transportation construction sector (9% on average in the last 5 years)
- Significant delays from Union Pacific Railroad approvals (over 3 years delayed)

## Fiscal responsibility

The City has a responsibility to balance this project against all other community services and long-term financial health. 

The cost escalations would require substantial redistribution of funds from other City services, possibly taking on additional debt, and could risk the City’s reserve funds. The City could not responsibly make the decision to proceed considering these risks to other services, especially with the potential for future unknown project cost factors.

## Next steps

The City remains committed to the initial intent of the 2018 ballot measure to improve safety and traffic flow through the corridor. 

In 2026, the City will restore the existing conditions from Kipling to Oak streets, including repaving and sidewalk replacement. For the long term, the City will continue to evaluate the feasibility and associated costs of an at-grade crossing and widening.

A recording of the January 20, 2026 [presentation about this decision and discussion with the City Council is available on the City's YouTube channel](https://youtu.be/5TKKoIW8FiM?si=60YF6BdUGQTBINIO&t=1106). Please find additional details below.

1. [February 2026 Community Update](#tabc79cc707-4d40-46f1-9232-6faa0b70af92_1)

1. [Letter from the City Manager](#tabc79cc707-4d40-46f1-9232-6faa0b70af92_2)

Dear Arvada Resident,

I'm writing to share some news about the W. 72nd Avenue project. After careful review, we’ve made the decision to cancel the underpass portion of the W. 72nd Avenue project.

In mid-December, the project team received final cost projections showing the underpass would cost more than double the original $64.5 million bond amount. While we anticipated significant cost increases, the final figures exceeded even our most conservative estimates.

Since then, the project team and City leadership have explored the most likely and feasible paths forward: reviewing line-by-line costs, negotiating with contractors, and evaluating funding options, including additional debt and reserve fund use. Ultimately, I recommended to the City Council canceling the underpass because continuing would not be fiscally responsible. The City Council agreed with this recommendation.

There are a few key factors behind this decision. Construction costs have increased substantially since 2018 due to extreme inflation—pressures we know many households and businesses are also facing. Significant approval delays from the Union Pacific Railroad pushed the timeline back by three years, and each delay was further compounded by inflation. Additionally, due to the complex underground work, there is high risk of further cost increases and once construction begins we are obligated to complete the project.

As City Manager, I have the responsibility to safeguard the City’s financial health, today and into the future. Advancing the project would require diverting resources from other critical needs and jeopardize our long-term stability. After weighing the costs, trade-offs, and funding shortfall, I could not in good conscience recommend moving forward with the current plan.

I recognize this change in direction is unexpected. The team has worked tirelessly on this project, including the completed improvements west of Oak on 72nd Avenue,  and on Ralston Road. I’ve directed the team to begin evaluating alternative approaches from Oak to Kipling, including widening the at-grade railroad crossing. We will keep the community informed as this effort progresses.

Thank you for your understanding. I remain committed to finding a solution that improves safety and mobility on W. 72nd Avenue in a way that is financially prudent.

Sincerely,

Don Wick

City Manager

1. [Frequently Asked Questions](#tabc79cc707-4d40-46f1-9232-6faa0b70af92_3)

### [FAQs](/Faq.aspx?TID=85)

[Why is the underpass being canceled?](#)
:   The latest cost estimate brought the project total to $137 million, more than double the $64.5 million bond amount allocated to W. 72nd Avenue. Continuing would require the City to find significant alternative funding sources, including taking on additional debt and deferring many other City projects for years. Additionally, once construction begins, the project must be completed. The City could not responsibly proceed given these risks to other services, especially considering the potential for future unknown cost factors due to the complex underground work.

[How much did costs increase?](#)
:   Voters approved $64.5 million of the 2018 bond package for the W. 72nd Avenue widening from Simms to Kipling streets. Prior to December 2025, the most recent estimate for the project was $97.5 million, which the City had incorporated into its 10-year financial model. In mid-December, the formal bid and independent cost estimate incorporating phase 3 brought the project total to $137 million, nearly $40 million over the previous estimate and more than double the original bond amount.

[Why did cost increase so significantly?](#)
:   Several factors drove the cost increase. Inflation in the transportation construction industry has been particularly extreme. Colorado indices show approximately 9% annual inflation since the 2018 bond approval, compared to a historical average of 2.6% (see graph). Additionally, the Union Pacific Railroad (UPRR) approvals took far longer than expected. While discussions had been underway for years, these approvals delayed phase three of the project by over 3 years. During that time, construction costs continued to rise.

    ![Quarterly CDOT construction cost indices increases 2012 to 2025 with 83% increase 2018 to 2025](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=7028)

[What happens to the unused bond money?](#)
:   Per the ballot measure, bond funds can only be used to improve the approved corridor from Simms to Kipling. Of the $64.5 million allocated to the W. 72nd project, $41 million has been spent on the completed work. Some remaining funds will restore the existing corridor from Oak to Kipling in 2026, including repaving. The rest will be held while the City evaluates the feasibility of an at-grade crossing. Should the City not move forward with any additional improvements, the funds can be used to repay the portion of the bond funds that have been spent.

    Taxes did not increase for the bond projects. The City took out a loan, as approved by voters in 2018, and is repaying it over time using existing tax revenue.

[Will any additional work be completed from Oak to Kipling?](#)
:   Yes, the corridor will be restored from the current interim conditions. Residents can expect active construction through the corridor this year. Work to be completed in 2026 includes:

    - Repaving existing W 72nd Ave. (Oak to Kipling)
    - Sidewalk replacement as needed
    - Oak St. intersection restoration and completion
    - Water line, sewer line, and drainage pipe installations
    - Miscellaneous repairs along the corridor (e.g., near Lincoln Academy)
    - Fence installation
    - Limited landscaping

    Please [visit the project webpage](https://www.arvadaco.gov/669/W-72nd-Avenue) and [sign up for the project email list](https://app.e2ma.net/app2/audience/signup/1967947/1717219/) for updates on timelines and construction impacts.

[Is widening the crossing at-grade possible, and how long would it take?](#)
:   An at-grade crossing is being evaluated. Since the current project was designed with the underpass, an at-grade option requires new design work and a new railroad approval process. This will likely take 5 to 10 years to complete design phases, obtain approvals, and move to construction. There are four design review phases (30%, 60%, 90%, and 100%), each requiring railroad approval before advancing. Each phase can take several months to years depending on complexity. At each phase, the City gains more accurate cost estimates to determine whether to continue.

    Some completed work can help accelerate the process. For example, the necessary right-of-way has been acquired from property owners along the corridor and utilities have been relocated.

[How was the decision made?](#)
:   The City team worked to understand all options that could help fund the project, including varying levels of debt, depleting reserve funds, and canceling other projects and priorities. With all of the options on the table, the City Manager determined that continuing the project was not fiscally responsible and posed too substantial a risk to other City services. City Council discussed and agreed with this decision. [Watch the January 20, 2026 Council workshop for details](https://youtu.be/5TKKoIW8FiM?si=60YF6BdUGQTBINIO&t=1106).

[What other funding options were considered to complete the project, and why weren’t they pursued?](#)
:   The City explored all funding options before making this decision. City staff and leadership looked at several ways to cover the increased cost: taking on more debt, using reserve funds, and diverting funds from other projects. In every case, the trade-offs were too steep. Continuing would have impacted too many other priorities. Taking on more debt could limit funds for other capital projects, affect operational budgets, and restrict flexibility to respond to future community needs. Reserve funds are intended to protect the City from financial unknowns and support service continuity during economic downturns or natural disasters.

    Additionally, due to the complex underground work, there is high risk of further cost increases and once construction begins we are obligated to complete the project. The City could not responsibly proceed given these risks and the potential for additional unknown project costs.

[When did the City receive the new cost estimates?](#)
:   The cost estimate was provided in mid-December 2025. The City then negotiated with the contractor and conducted an independent cost estimating process to lower the estimate as much as possible. In the weeks that followed, the City began discussing the feasibility of continuing the underpass portion of the project.

/FAQ.aspx

## Learn more

Listen to the Inside Arvada podcast episode about the decision not to move forward with the underpass on the project using the player below or wherever you listen to podcasts, including [Buzzsprout](https://www.buzzsprout.com/2320363/episodes/18637523-inside-arvada-s-changes-to-the-w-72nd-avenue-project) (with transcript).

## Timeline

\*Updated January 2026

- **2018:**voters approve West 72 Avenue and Ralston Road bond projects
- **2021 to 2022:**Phase 1 Utility Work
- **2022 to 2024:**Phase 2 Swadley to Oak Street construction (spring)
- **2024 to 2025:**Project paused during railroad approval process
- **2026:**Underpass canceled due to cost escalation and alternative improvements under evaluation, including an at-grade crossing
- **2026 to 2027:**restoration work from Oak to Kipling, including repaving and sidewalk replacement
- **Ongoing evaluation (TBD):**alternative improvements from Oak to Kipling

1. [Project Background](#tabee8bba1d-a8df-4436-aa7f-93e33d31629e_0)

- In the November 6, 2018 election, Arvada residents approved Ballot Issue 3F for a bond issue to fund improvements to Ralston Road and W 72nd Avenue.
- W. 72nd Avenue is a major east-west corridor for Arvada, serving 21,000 vehicle trips each day. This regional corridor provides access to Westminster and Golden /Jefferson County.
- The Citizens' Capital Improvement Plan Committee (CCIPC) ranked improvements to W 72nd Avenue as a high priority.
- The project also meets concerns expressed in recent Arvada Citizen Surveys.
- The [2014 Comprehensive Plan](/307/2014-Comprehensive-Plan) generated transportation models indicating that the congestion, operation and safety of W 72nd Avenue will deteriorate with the build-out of the City.

1. [Improvement Needs](#tabee8bba1d-a8df-4436-aa7f-93e33d31629e_1)

- West of Kipling St., W 72nd Avenue shrinks from four lanes to two, creating a bottleneck
- The at-grade Union Pacific Railroad crossing near Oak St. creates traffic backups when a train passes through
- The intermittent or absent sidewalks create unsafe conditions for pedestrians and cyclists

1. [Planned Improvements](#tabee8bba1d-a8df-4436-aa7f-93e33d31629e_2)

Updated 1/21/26

- Widen W 72nd Avenue between Kipling and Simms Streets
  - The underpass portion has been canceled due to cost escalation. Alternative improvements from Kipling to Oak are being evaluated, including an at-grade widening and crossing.
- Add bike lanes and sidewalks
- Upgrade signalized intersections
- Resolve significant drainage issues along W 72nd Avenue

1. [Council Presentations](#tabee8bba1d-a8df-4436-aa7f-93e33d31629e_3)

The City team presents to the City Council with updates about the bond projects at W 72nd Avenue and Ralston Road.
